title: Sigma-algebras and Borel sets

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: On the Hilbert space of square-integrable functions on the interval from zero to one, multiplication by the coordinate x has the whole interval as spectrum but no eigenvectors.
body: A spectral projection associated with a subset of the interval should keep a function on that subset and set it to zero elsewhere. We now face a foundational question: which subsets can be selected? And why should we insist on a collection closed under infinitely many set operations? The answer begins with a sigma-algebra.

slides.title: Why finite set operations are insufficient
slides.lead: Think first about an event such as a number lying between two endpoints.
body: We may want its complement: the number lies outside that interval. We may want the union of several intervals. These are ordinary finite set operations. But spectral approximations introduce limits. Suppose we select the union of the intervals from one over n to one, with n ranging over positive integers. The union is the interval strictly above zero and at most one. No finite stage equals that union. Or suppose we intersect the intervals from negative one over n to positive one over n. Their common intersection is the singleton containing zero.

slides.title: Three elementary examples
slides.lead: The smallest sigma-algebra on a set contains only the empty set and the whole set.
body: It can distinguish nothing within the space. The largest sigma-algebra is the power set: every subset is allowed. On a finite set, this choice is harmless and often the default. Between them lie many other sigma-algebras. For example, partition a set of four points into the pair one and two, and the pair three and four. Allow only the empty set, the whole set, and the two pairs. Complements exchange the pairs, and countable unions cannot produce a singleton. This family is a sigma-algebra. It represents a limited ability to distinguish events.

slides.title: Generating a sigma-algebra
slides.lead: Given a collection of subsets, consider all sigma-algebras containing them.
body: Their intersection is itself a sigma-algebra: the whole space is in every family, complements stay in every family, and so do countable unions. Therefore there is a smallest sigma-algebra containing the original collection. We call it the sigma-algebra generated by that collection. The Borel sigma-algebra of the real line is the sigma-algebra generated by all open subsets. This definition immediately includes closed sets, because complements of open sets are closed. It includes open and closed intervals, half-open intervals, and singleton points.

slides.title: Why open sets are a good starting point
slides.lead: Continuity already tells us how open sets behave.
body: A function f between topological spaces is continuous precisely when the preimage of every open set is open. A measurable function is defined similarly, except the preimage of an open set need only be in the domain's sigma-algebra. The codomain may be the real or complex numbers with their Borel sigma-algebras. Because preimages commute with complements and countable unions, checking preimages of open sets is enough to ensure that preimages of all Borel sets are measurable. This is a compact but powerful argument. Let F be the family of target sets whose preimages are measurable. F is a sigma-algebra.

slides.title: Indicators and step functions
slides.lead: For a set E, define its indicator to be one on E and zero outside.
body: It is measurable exactly when E is measurable, in the usual real-valued setting. To see the forward direction, take the preimage of an open neighborhood of one that excludes zero. To see the reverse, note that the preimage of any open subset of the real line is one of four sets: empty, whole, E, or its complement. A finite linear combination of indicators of measurable sets is a simple function. Such functions take only finitely many values. Their role in integration is similar to the role of step functions in basic calculus.

slides.title: Boundary points matter
slides.lead: Consider the sets of spectral values strictly below a threshold and those at or below it.
body: Their difference is the singleton at the threshold. In the multiplication-by-x model on an interval with Lebesgue measure, that singleton has measure zero. So the two indicator operators act identically on L two functions, because they differ only on a null set. For a diagonal operator with a genuine eigenvector at the threshold, the singleton projection can be nonzero. Then the open and closed spectral cuts differ by the entire corresponding eigenspace. This is why we must retain exact endpoint conventions in a perturbation theorem.

slides.title: Countable addition and the future spectral measure
slides.lead: Suppose E-one, E-two, and so forth are pairwise disjoint Borel sets.
body: Their union is Borel. A projection-valued spectral measure should assign a projection to each set in a way compatible with such disjoint unions. But we must be careful about the type of convergence. The sum of the projections need not converge in operator norm. For example, projections onto successive coordinate axes in ell two have partial sums that approach the identity on every individual vector, while the operator-norm distance from any finite partial sum to the identity remains one.

slides.title: A preview of bounded Borel calculus
slides.lead: Continuous functional calculus can apply continuous functions to a self-adjoint operator.
body: Indicators of intervals are generally discontinuous, so they are not covered by that construction alone. A bounded Borel calculus admits bounded measurable functions as symbols. It includes indicators and therefore spectral projections. It also respects addition, multiplication, and adjoints in the appropriate operator algebra. A spectral projection of a set is defined only for sets in the measurable class of the spectral measure, usually the Borel sets. This restriction determines which spectral selections functional calculus supports.
